records.title: Configuration-to-Performance Scaling Law with Neural Ansatz

records.abstract: Training Large Language Models (LLMs) is prohibitively expensive, creating a critical scaling gap where insights from small-scale experiments often fail to transfer to resource-intensive production systems, thereby hindering efficient innovation. To bridge this, we introduce Farseer, a novel and refined scaling law offering enhanced predictive accuracy across scales. By systematically constructing a model loss surface $L(N,D)$, Farseer achieves a significantly better fit to empirical data than prior laws (e.g., Chinchilla's law). Our methodology yields accurate, robust, and highly generalizable predictions, demonstrating excellent extrapolation capabilities, improving upon Chinchilla's law by reducing extrapolation error by 433\%. This allows for the reliable evaluation of competing training strategies across all $(N,D)$ settings, enabling conclusions from small-scale ablation studies to
records.title: Predictable Scale: Part II, Farseer: A Refined Scaling Law in Large Language Models

records.abstract: Face representation is a crucial step of face recognition systems. An optimal face representation should be discriminative, robust, compact, and very easy-to-implement. While numerous hand-crafted and learning-based representations have been proposed, considerable room for improvement is still present. In this paper, we present a very easy-to-implement deep learning framework for face representation. Our method bases on a new structure of deep network (called Pyramid CNN). The proposed Pyramid CNN adopts a greedy-filter-and-down-sample operation, which enables the training procedure to be very fast and computation-efficient. In addition, the structure of Pyramid CNN can naturally incorporate feature sharing across multi-scale face representations, increasing the discriminative ability of resulting representation. records.title: Learning Deep Face Representation

records.abstract: Foundation models are increasingly trained on sequences of user actions in recommendation, payments, fraud, and commerce, but these models still lack the kind of compute calibration that scaling laws provide for language models. We study a common two-part behavioral-model architecture: a feature-based event embedder maps each multi-modal item to a vector, and a decoder-only transformer predicts the next event from the resulting sequence. Across roughly 600 runs on real interaction data, spanning $10^{15}$-$10^{19}$ training FLOPs, we jointly vary four deployment-relevant axes: the two-part parameter split, critical batch size, model/data allocation, and the number of sampled negatives used after freezing the embedder. records.title: Scaling Laws for Behavioral Foundation Models over User Event Sequences

registration_notes.N91.1: This is a SURVEY for a measurement-context question - not a claim audit, and NOT a novelty search. The hypothesis is that the joint scaling conclusion IS already established (scaling laws); the survey documents the displacing/presence evidence, not an absence.
registration_notes.N91.2: Question registered before search: is the finding 'model-size scaling saturates, data scaling saturates, but scaling BOTH jointly improves past the individual limits' already investigated and confirmed in the literature?
registration_notes.N91.3: Anchors are recall probes: each MUST be retrieved by a topic query that does NOT contain its title, else the search is insensitive and every 'not found' is worthless.
registration_notes.N91.4: Query families are phrased to find the presence of joint-scaling work (Chinchilla-style compute-optimal scaling, data-saturation, width/parameter saturation, kernel/RF joint theory), not work that merely agrees in spirit.
registration_notes.N91.5: Empty queries are recorded, not dropped. Rate-limited queries are retried and residual failures recorded separately from genuinely empty results.
registration_notes.N91.6: This survey expects PRESENCE. A positive result (retrieving Chinchilla/Kaplan/Muennighoff-class work) confirms the user's suspicion; absence would be UNRESOLVED, never 'first'.
registration_notes.N91.7: Title/abstract mark a source live; only primary text with a located passage may count as displacement.
